Every section was read: abstract, §1 intro, §2 setup, §3 adaptive submodularity (Defs 1-2, Prop 3), §4 greedy guarantee (Thm 4), §5 stochastic submodular maximization (Thm 5), §6 adaptive viral marketing (Thm 6), §7 active learning (Thm 7, Prop 8), §8 hardness (Thm 9), conclusions, references. extraction.research_question: When can a simple adaptive greedy policy be guaranteed near-optimal for stochastic optimization under partial observability, where feasible solutions are decision policies rather than sets? The paper defines adaptive submodularity as the policy-level analog of diminishing returns and asks which applications satisfy it (sensor placement with failures, adaptive viral marketing, pool-based active learning). It also asks how hard the general problem is without that property (§8).
extraction.theory: Submodular set-function theory (Nemhauser, Wolsey & Fisher 1978) extended to policies. The key condition is that playing layer j of a policy tree earlier cannot decrease its marginal contribution (Def 2, Eq. 4). Equivalent form: for subrealizations Psi subset Psi', the expected marginal gain satisfies Delta_Psi'(e) <= Delta_Psi(e) (Prop 3, §3). Adaptive monotonicity is Def 1 (§3). Closure under nonnegative combinations and truncation is stated in §3.
extraction.data: No dataset. Applications are analytic. (a) Sensor placement: finite location set E, sensor states O, independent failures P[Phi] = prod_e P[Phi(e)] (§5, p.6). (b) Adaptive viral marketing: directed graph G=(V,A) under the independent cascade model, with myopic or full-adoption feedback (§6, p.7). (c) Pool-based active learning: unlabeled pool X, finite hypothesis set H with prior p_H, binary or multi-class labels, no label noise (§7, p.8). No sample sizes, N, or period are reported.
extraction.method: Analytic proofs only. Definitions of adaptive monotonicity and submodularity (Defs 1-2); derivative characterization (Prop 3, proof by constructing a path-shaped policy tree); greedy guarantee (Thm 4) via a telescoping argument adapted from Nemhauser et al. (1978) and Goundan & Schulz (2007); instantiations for three applications (Thm 5, Thm 6, Prop 8 / Thm 7); hardness via a reduction using a permanent-based puzzle and Feige & Lund (1997) (Thm 9).
extraction.identification: Not applicable. There is no estimation or causal identification. The guarantees are worst-case bounds conditional on the prior P[Phi] and on the utility being adaptive submodular.
extraction.scope: Population: none (no empirical units). Institution: none. Era: 2010 preprint. Domain: adaptive stochastic maximization and coverage, with examples in sensor placement, independent-cascade viral marketing (Kempe et al. 2003 model), and Bayesian pool-based active learning. Nothing in the text touches lobbying, elections, campaigns, legislators, persuasion or turnout, or text measurement. The only network-relevant content is §6 (influence spread on a directed graph with edge probabilities), which bears on seed allocation under a budget k.

key_findings.finding: Under adaptive monotonicity and adaptive submodularity, the alpha-approximate greedy policy achieves at least (1 - e^{-l/(alpha k)}) of the expected reward of the best policy with k items; with l = k and alpha = 1 this is the classic (1 - 1/e) guarantee.

key_findings.finding: Sensor placement with multiple failure types (not only all-or-nothing failure) under independent failures is adaptive submodular, so the adaptive greedy policy achieves (1 - 1/e) of the best adaptive policy when the base objective f-hat is monotone submodular. This extends Asadpour et al. (2008).

key_findings.finding: Adaptive viral marketing under the independent cascade model is adaptive submodular for any nonnegative monotone submodular reward over influenced nodes, under both myopic and full-adoption feedback. summary_md:
Golovin and Krause extend the classic greedy guarantee for submodular sets (Nemhauser et al. 1978) to adaptive policies. In their setting you pick an item, observe its random outcome, and only then pick the next. Two properties are required. Adaptive monotonicity (Def 1) means an added item never lowers the expected reward. Adaptive submodularity (Prop 3) means an item's expected marginal gain only shrinks as more outcomes are observed. When both hold, the adaptive greedy policy achieves at least (1 - e^{-l/(alpha k)}) of the best k-item policy (Thm 4). With alpha = 1 and l = k this is 1 - 1/e, about 0.632. If marginals are estimated with additive error epsilon, the bound loses l*epsilon. The paper applies the result to three problems: sensors with independent failures (Thm 5), adaptive seeding under the independent cascade (Thm 6), and Bayesian active learning, where it gives an OPT*(ln(1/min p_H)+1) bound (Thm 7). Without adaptive submodularity, the general problem cannot be approximated within O(|E|^{1-epsilon/beta}) (Thm 9). This is a 13-page theory preprint with no data.

What it means for Paul's system: the CU budget optimizer and the frontier both run lazy greedy, but neither is adaptive in the paper's sense. Nothing is observed. Seed take-up is drawn inside Monte Carlo, and "conversions" are deterministic modeled transitions. The optimizer already scopes its claims correctly. In a fixed stance state it is exact (separable and concave), and once a conversion can happen it reports no guarantee, which Thm 9 supports. The sharpest finding is in the dashboard's budgetRecruit. It claims the full (1-1/e), but because it multiplies each candidate's gain by a target-proximity weight in [1,3], Thm 4 only supports about 0.28 when a target is set. The paper also defines the step the system has not built: seed one member, observe whether they took up the ask (SGATE), then re-plan.

bearings.paper_claim: Under adaptive monotonicity and adaptive submodularity, the alpha-approximate adaptive greedy gets >= (1 - e^{-l/(alpha k)}) of the best policy (1-1/e at alpha=1, l=k). Without adaptive submodularity, Adaptive Stochastic Maximization is inapproximable within O(|E|^{1-epsilon/beta}) unless PH = Sigma2P, even for pointwise-linear objectives.
bearings.system_side: The optimizer runs CELF lazy greedy in $500 steps. In a fixed stance state it certifies the exact grid optimum (separable, verified concave) and reports 1-1/e only as a 'worst_case_submodular_floor'. When a modeled money-triggered conversion is reachable, it rebuilds the queue, reports guarantee kind 'none', and explicitly refuses to call the run an observed adaptive policy. The G-K data-dependent bound is cited as 'JAIR'11 Lemma 5.3 / A.9'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's adaptive guarantee needs a random state Phi that the policy observes, plus adaptive submodularity. The optimizer has no observation step: conversions are deterministic model thresholds. So Thm 4 does not apply to the replanning mode, and Thm 9's hardness explains why no guarantee should be claimed there. The code already does this. In fixed-state mode, separable concavity gives exactness, which is stronger than the paper's bound, so the paper adds nothing there. The cited Lemma 5.3/A.9 is not in this 13-page text. It belongs to the extended JAIR version (golovin-2011-adaptive-submodularity-theory).

bearings.paper_claim: An alpha-approximate greedy rule (each pick's marginal >= 1/alpha of the best marginal) only guarantees (1 - e^{-l/(alpha k)}) of optimal. The full (1-1/e) requires alpha = 1.
bearings.paper_location: Thm 4 and Def of alpha-approximate greedy, §4 p.5 (lines 256-259)
bearings.system_side: budgetRecruit maximizes a monotone submodular coverage sum_u [1 - prod(1-p)], and its comment claims 'the classic greedy keeps the (1-1/e)≈0.63 guarantee'. When a target is given, though, each candidate's true coverage marginal g is multiplied by (1 + 2*dT[c]). Here dT is max-product proximity in (0,1], so the multiplier lies in [1,3] and greedy picks argmax of weighted gain rather than of true marginal.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Pure math, so it carries over directly. With the target weighting, the chosen item's true marginal is >= 1/3 of the best, so alpha <= 3. Thm 4 then supports only about 1 - e^{-1/3} ≈ 0.28 of optimal coverage, not 0.63. With no target (dT null), the 1-1/e claim holds for this one-hop coverage objective. Note that the objective counts only one-hop coverage, not cascade spread. UNVERIFIED (agent analysis, single path, DE-062).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-pathfinding#Best-sponsor, multi-target tree and budget max-coverage modes|Best-sponsor, multi-target tree and budget max-coverage modes]]

bearings.paper_claim: Greedy computed with additive marginal error epsilon guarantees (1 - e^{-l/k})·OPT - l·epsilon. Adaptive seeding is adaptive submodular (hence 1-1/e) for the single-colour independent cascade with any monotone submodular reward, under myopic or full-adoption feedback.
bearings.paper_location: §4 p.5 text after Thm 4 (lines 339-346); Thm 6, §6 p.7
bearings.system_side: The frontier runs lazy greedy up to 60 seeds on a Monte Carlo spread (MC=20, CRN). The spread comes from a two-colour competitive race with money-driven anti bystanders and seeds gated by contingent take-up. The marginal is max(0, sp - cur)*fac[c], with leverage and contest factors. Seeds are chosen before any take-up is observed, and the display curve is clamped because MC dips occur.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Thm 6 covers only single-colour IC. The frontier's competitive race with anti bystanders, plus the per-candidate fac weights, puts it outside that guarantee (see Bharathi/Borodin on competitive models). Even where submodularity held, the MC=20 noise in each marginal enters the bound as a -l*epsilon term over up to 60 seeds. The observed MC dips mean epsilon is not negligible. The knee should be read as a heuristic, not a certified diminishing-returns point.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-allocation#Budget frontier with knee and electoral modes|Budget frontier with knee and electoral modes]]

bearings.paper_claim: When items fail independently (P[Phi] = prod_e P[Phi(e)]), and failure has multiple outcome types, the problem is adaptive submodular. Adaptive greedy, which places an item, observes its state, then continues, achieves (1-1/e) of the best ADAPTIVE policy (Thm 5). Adaptive seeding with feedback is likewise adaptive submodular (Thm 6).
bearings.system_side: gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob·SGATE[tier]) gives each lobbied seed a take-up probability. It is drawn independently per member on a dedicated CRN stream. The allocator never conditions later choices on whether earlier seeds actually took up the ask.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The gate already has the 'sensor with independent failure' structure that Thm 5 covers. An observe-then-replan policy (lobby, see whether the member moved, choose the next) would fall under the paper's guarantee, but only if take-up is independent across members and the reward stays adaptive submodular. In real Congresses, party whips and coalition timing correlate take-up, which violates the independence premise. SGATE values are themselves unestimated.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Contingent seed activation gate|Contingent seed activation gate]]

bearings.paper_claim: Kempe et al.'s expected-spread function is submodular, and the greedy guarantee applies to greedy SEQUENTIAL selection on true marginals (Thm 4 generalizes Nemhauser's greedy).
bearings.system_side: The coalition allocator computes SINGLETON marginals spread({n}) - base for the top-45, boosts them by (1+0.8 bpf), and water-fills dollars. It then honestly reports the joint spread against the naive-additive sum, because spread is submodular.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Reporting joint spread is correct and is consistent with submodularity. However, the allocation itself is not greedy on conditional marginals, so no (1-1/e) guarantee from this paper, or from Nemhauser, attaches to the per-topic seed sets. They are diagnostics, and the code already treats them as non-summable.

bearings.paper_claim: Once diminishing returns fail, no polynomial policy approximates the optimum within O(|E|^{1-epsilon/beta}) in the worst case (Thm 9). The positive results require adaptive submodularity.
bearings.system_side: Cheapest-tip LT priming sorts recruits greedily by $/influence-unit against tier thresholds theta. Threshold adoption is not submodular in general, and the code makes no approximation claim.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a worst-case statement only. It explains why no guarantee should be attached to LT priming or to any variant where pressure is non-diminishing. It says nothing about how typical instances on the cosponsor graph behave.

gaps_exposed: No observe-then-replan (adaptive) allocation. Seed take-up (SGATE) is only ever simulated inside Monte Carlo, never observed between choices, so the paper's adaptive guarantee, which compares against the best adaptive policy, is out of reach for every built allocator.
budgetRecruit's (1-1/e) comment ignores the alpha-approximation penalty from its (1+2*dT) target weighting. The supportable bound is about 0.28 when a target is set.
The Monte Carlo marginal error epsilon (MC=20, observed dips) is never bounded or propagated into the frontier's knee or guarantee language, even though Thm 4's corollary shows it costs l*epsilon.

No allocator tests whether its objective is adaptive submodular. The competitive two-colour race with anti bystanders falls outside Thm 6, and the system has no empirical check for diminishing returns on the spread objective; the optimizer checks concavity only for its own fixed-state separable objective.
The extended JAIR version (holding the data-dependent bound the code cites) is a separate document; the optimizer's citation 'JAIR'11 Lemma 5.3 / A.9' cannot be verified from this text.

Overclaim in the dashboard: make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:775-776 states the (1-1/e)≈0.63 guarantee for budgetRecruit. Under Thm 4 the target-weighted mode supports only about 1 - e^{-1/3} ≈ 0.28. UNVERIFIED (single agent path, DE-062) until reproduced.

Paul's Chen 2023 margin note says pressure from high-ranking members is 'not diminishing'. If that holds, adaptive submodularity fails and Thm 9's hardness applies, so any greedy (1-1/e) language on cascade-based allocators would be unsupported.
No conflict with the barred SNA proposals: the paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, and it makes no LDA or reciprocity claims.
paul_alignment: The evidence partly agrees with Paul, and his note is somewhat stale. He calls 'adaptive greedy plus CELF' the operational layer. The built optimizer uses CELF lazy greedy, but it is deliberately NOT adaptive. In a fixed stance state it is exact through separable concavity, which is stronger than Golovin-Krause, so the adaptive guarantee adds nothing there. In conversion mode it correctly claims no guarantee, which Thm 9 supports. The truly adaptive piece the paper describes would be lobbying, observing contingent take-up (the SGATE draw) and re-planning. That is not built, and the system's own docstring says so. Paul's expectation that GCOMB-style learned policies will replace greedy is outside this paper. His positions on per-topic-allocators and budget-frontier, which place them in a 'static and submodular tier', are partly right: the coalition allocator is not greedy on conditional marginals, and the frontier's competitive objective is not proven submodular.

related.why: This is the longer JAIR version with the same arXiv ID. It holds the proofs, cost extensions and the data-dependent bound (Lemma 5.3/A.9) that fec/engine/optimize.py cites.
Contingency-aware seeding, the basis of SGATE, is the adaptive-feedback setting that Golovin-Krause Thm 5/6 analyze, with independent take-up failures.

Its empirical challenge to greedy in IM is a counterweight to the worst-case greedy guarantees here. The dashboard uses PageRank on that basis.

extraction.venue: Annual Review of Psychology, 54:547-77 (first published online as a Review in Advance, August 14, 2002)

extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 1,681 numbered lines of the extracted text, covering article pp. 547-572 and the reference list pp. 573-577. The text file on disk is 99,003 bytes, not the 97,932 characters stated in the task hint; the metadata hint was correct. Studies summarized in the review were not read separately; their numbers are as reported by the authors.
extraction.research_question: Can natural word use (open-ended speech and writing, read as style rather than content) serve as a reliable individual-difference marker and as a window onto social, situational, psychological and health processes; and which methods of counting words are available and useful (stated at p. 548)?
extraction.theory: Word use is treated as a psychological marker, with the strongest emphasis on function words ("particles": pronouns, articles, prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliary verbs). The authors argue particles encode shared reference, social identity and self-focus, and cognitive style. Background traditions cited include psychoanalysis (Freud 1901; Lacan 1968), Ricoeur's account of how descriptions define meaning, Goffman's dramaturgy, politeness theory (Brown & Levinson 1987), communication accommodation theory, and verbal immediacy (Wiener & Mehrabian 1968). The review says no compelling psychological theory of word usage yet exists (p. 572). Narrative-writing and disclosure theory (Pennebaker & Francis 1996) is used to explain health effects through coherent narrative construction and shifts in perspective.
extraction.data: None collected by the authors. The review summarizes evidence from many sources: General Inquirer and LIWC studies; Biber's corpus of 481 texts (about 1,000,000 words) across 23 genres (p. 554); Pennebaker & King (1999) writing samples from diaries, college essays and journal abstracts (p. 555); Mehl & Pennebaker (2002a) electronically activated recorder (EAR) samples of everyday conversation from 52 college students (p. 557); a cross-sectional age analysis of more than 3,000 participants from 45 studies, 21 labs and 3 countries, plus 10 authors (p. 556); Mulac et al. (2001) review of more than 30 gender studies (p. 557); Pennebaker & King (1999) Big Five correlations; Newman et al. (2002) five laboratory deception studies (p. 564); Giuliani's 14 press conferences during his first 5 years in office (p. 565); about 15 students wearing EARs after September 11, 2001 (p. 566); Princess Diana online chat groups (p. 566). Sample sizes for most cited health and clinical studies are not reported in the review. Periods covered span roughly 1941 to 2002, with many citations marked "submitted", "in press" or unpublished.
extraction.method: Narrative review organized in sections: (1) six word-count and pattern-analysis methods (General Inquirer, TAS/C, Weintraub's verbal analysis, DICTION, LIWC, Biber factor analysis; LSA as a pattern approach), pp. 549-555; (2) psychometric reliability of word use, pp. 555-556; (3) demographic, personality, mood, need-state, self-esteem and psychopathology links, pp. 556-562; (4) situational, social, deception, upheaval and marital links, pp. 562-567; (5) word use and psychological and health change, including LIWC-based writing-intervention analyses and LSA pronoun-shift analyses, pp. 567-570; (6) discussion of which word classes to study and limitations, pp. 570-572. The review does not pool effects statistically and reports most effects as correlations, percentages or qualitative patterns.
extraction.identification: Not applicable. The review contains no causal identification strategy of its own. Causal language is used loosely in places (e.g., pronoun use "predicting" health changes, p. 569), and the authors note bidirectional effects, particularly in social accommodation (p. 558).
extraction.scope: Psychology, primarily English-language and largely US-based work, with some European and cross-cultural studies cited. Participants are mostly college students, clinical or patient samples, disclosure-study volunteers, public figures (Giuliani, Watergate transcripts, US presidents), novelists and poets, and online chat or everyday-conversation samples. The authors explicitly say they do not cover non-English languages, spoken versus written differences in depth, second-language learners or intelligence (p. 573). Political and campaign speech is discussed only briefly (Hart's DICTION, presidential speeches, Winter 1973, Zullow et al. 1988; pp. 552-553). Nothing on lobbying, legislators, elections, networks or allocation is presented as a finding.

key_findings.finding: Word-use measures show temporal stability. Across 21 language categories in 5-minute talks, successive 2-minute intervals correlated on average at 0.51 (Gleser et al. 1959). Students' everyday conversation was re-sampled four weeks apart with test-retest r of 0.41 for standard linguistic variables and 0.24 for psychological-process variables.
key_findings.location: Psychometric Properties of Word Use, pp. 555-556
key_findings.numbers: r = 0.51 (21 categories, 2-min intervals); r = 0.41 standard variables, r = 0.24 psychological processes (EAR, Mehl & Pennebaker 2002a)

key_findings.finding: Word use is consistent across topic and social context, so it can be treated as an individual-difference measure. Pennebaker & King (1999) found good internal consistency across text types for 36 LIWC dimensions, and word use was stable across home versus public and work versus amusement settings.
key_findings.location: Psychometric Properties of Word Use, pp. 555-556
key_findings.numbers: 36 LIWC dimensions; text samples from diaries, essays and abstracts written across days and years

key_findings.finding: Language changes with age. Older participants used more positive and fewer negative emotion words, fewer first-person singular references, more future tense and fewer past-tense verbs, and more cognitive-complexity words. Both the cross-sectional study and the novelist/poet longitudinal study converged.
key_findings.numbers: More than 3,000 participants, 45 studies, 21 labs, 3 countries; 60 text dimensions; 10 authors

key_findings.finding: Gender differences in word use are reported across studies, but the evidence is uneven. Mulac et al. (2001) found relatively unambiguous effects for 16 features; men used more quantity references, judgmental adjectives, directives and I-references, while women used more intensifiers, emotion references, uncertainty verbs, negations and hedges. Tag questions showed no consistent difference. In everyday conversations of 52 students, men used nearly four times as many swear words, and women used more filler words and positive-emotion references.
key_findings.numbers: More than 30 studies, 16 features; 52 college students (EAR); men about 4x swear words

key_findings.finding: Big Five self-reports correlate only modestly with word use. Pennebaker & King (1999) reported correlations of 0.10 to 0.16. Neuroticism related to more negative and fewer positive emotion words and more first-person singular; extraversion to positive emotion and social-process words; agreeableness to more positive and fewer negative emotion words.
key_findings.location: Traditional Personality Measures, The Big Five, p. 559
key_findings.numbers: r = 0.10 to 0.16 (Pennebaker & King 1999, multiple writing samples from several hundred college students)

key_findings.finding: Judges' ratings of text emotionality correlated more strongly with language than writers' or speakers' self-reported emotionality did, which raises the question of which personality 'gold standard' to rely on.
key_findings.numbers: Two studies cited (Pennebaker & Francis 1996; Berry et al. 1997); no coefficients given in the review

key_findings.finding: Depression and mania are linked to elevated first-person singular use. Currently depressed students used more I (not me/my/mine) in personal essays. Suicidal poets used fewer first-person plural and more first-person singular pronouns and more death words than nonsuicidal poets. Manic patients used first-person singular more often. The review reads this as self-preoccupation.
key_findings.location: Mental Health and Psychopathology, Depression and Suicidality, pp. 560-561
key_findings.numbers: 18 suicidal and nonsuicidal poets (Stirman & Pennebaker 2001); 10 manic patients (Lorenz & Cobb 1952); sample for Rude et al. (2002) not given in review

key_findings.finding: Physical health links are sparse but suggestive. First-person singular use in structured Type A interviews (self-involvement) related to coronary outcomes and remained significant after controlling for age, cholesterol, smoking and Type A behavior. Positive emotion words in autobiographical sketches from nuns predicted longer life expectancy.
key_findings.location: Physical Health and Health Behavior, pp. 561-562
key_findings.numbers: Scherwitz and colleagues (no effect sizes given); 80 nuns (Danner et al. 2001; no effect sizes given)

key_findings.finding: Deception shows word-level signatures. Across five laboratory studies, truth-tellers used more first-person singular pronouns and more exclusive words (but, except, without) than liars, and liars showed slight but consistent elevations in negative emotion words.
key_findings.numbers: Five laboratory studies (Newman et al. 2002); effect sizes not reported in review

key_findings.finding: Shared and personal upheavals shift pronoun use. After Princess Diana's death, first-person plural in chat groups rose 135% and I fell 12% for about a week, returning to normal by 10 days. In the weeks after September 11, students' first-person plural rose and first-person singular fell for at least 5 days. Texas A&M bonfire coverage doubled first-person plural and negative emotion words and cut big words by more than 10%. During personal crises, Giuliani's first-person singular almost tripled in the period after his diagnosis and related events.
key_findings.location: Emotional Upheavals, Personal and Shared Upheavals, pp. 565-566
key_findings.numbers: +135% first-person plural, -12% I (Diana chat groups); about 15 students (EAR, 9/11); doubling of first-person plural (Texas A&M); 14 press conferences (Giuliani, first 5 years)

key_findings.finding: Social interaction and marriage show word-level coordination and relational markers. Highly involved strangers used more certainty expressions, verbal immediacy and relational pronouns. Chat-room dyads matched each other's function-word and affect-word use turn by turn. Satisfied, traditional married couples used more we and less I.
key_findings.numbers: 120 participants (Cegala 1989); Sillars et al. (1997) large married-couple sample, numbers not given in review

key_findings.finding: Expressive writing about emotional upheavals improves health, and the best predictor is a rise in cognitive words over the writing days. Positive emotion words were linearly related to health gains, while negative emotion words showed an inverted-U relation. Changes in cognitive words explained more variance in health improvement than emotion words. Three independent labs reported related effects, including lymphocyte counts and working memory up to 12 weeks.
key_findings.location: Word Use as a Reflection of Psychological and Health Change, pp. 567-569
key_findings.numbers: Writing typically 3-5 days, 15-30 min/day; six writing studies (Pennebaker et al. 1997); Petrie et al. (1999) medical students; Klein & Boals (2001) working memory

key_findings.finding: Pronoun style, not content, tracks health. Day-to-day pronoun shifts among trauma writers correlated 0.3 to 0.5 with changes in physician visits across three studies. LSA content similarity between days showed no relation to health in three writing studies.
key_findings.location: References to Self and Others, pp. 569-570
key_findings.numbers: r = 0.3 to 0.5 (three studies, Campbell & Pennebaker 2002); LSA: no relation (three studies)

key_findings.finding: Particles dominate word use and are the most psychologically informative. Fewer than 200 common particles account for over half of the words people use, and emotion words are under 5% of words in speech and writing, so emotion-word counts predict emotional state weakly.
key_findings.location: Which Words Should We Be Studying?, pp. 570-571
key_findings.numbers: Under 200 particles = over 50% of words; emotion words under 5% of words

key_findings.finding: Word-count methods differ in scope: Biber's factor analysis of 481 texts (about 1,000,000 words) from 23 genres yielded 6 factors; LIWC searches over 2,300 words in more than 70 dimensions; DICTION uses 10,000 search words with 5 master variables and 35 subfeatures, normed on 20,000 samples; TAS/C uses about 2,000 emotion words and 3,900 abstraction entries. Word-count methods are reliable and efficient but ignore context, irony and sarcasm.
key_findings.numbers: Biber 481 texts / ~1,000,000 words / 23 genres / 67 variables / 6 factors; LIWC 2,300+ words / 70+ dimensions; DICTION 10,000 words / 5 master variables / 35 subfeatures / 20,000 norm samples; TAS/C 2,000+ / 3,900

limitations: Word counts cannot capture context, irony, sarcasm or multiple word meanings, and many communication constructs (ingroup-outgroup status, formality, requests) are not easily detected (pp. 572-573).
No compelling psychological theory of word usage yet exists (p. 572); Zeldow & McAdams (1993) questioned whether lower-level word counts have psychological meaning.
Gender findings rest on a few studies with small samples and one text source; several key claims come from exclusively nonpersonal writings (pp. 557-558).
Gender effects may reflect social engagement or power rather than sex, and language use may show bidirectional effects, e.g., accommodation to partners (pp. 558, 555-558).
Personality self-report correlations are small (r about 0.10-0.16) and are not clearly superior to judge ratings (pp. 559-560).
Clinical studies are often small, use inconsistent inclusion criteria, and lack proper control groups (pp. 560-561).
Health-linked evidence is sparse, often unpublished or submitted, and effect sizes are not reported for several key studies (pp. 561-562).
Unclear whether a sample predicting one outcome (e.g., positive words in an essay) generalizes to psychological or physical phenomena more broadly (p. 562).
Content-based dictionaries have performed poorly because topics are almost infinite and categories are culture-bound (p. 571).
Review omits cross-language comparison, written versus spoken differences in depth, second-language learning, intelligence and stereotype communication (p. 573).
Several cited studies are 'submitted', 'in press' or unpublished, so their results could not be checked against final publications from this text alone.

summary_md:
Pennebaker, Mehl and Niederhoffer (2003) is a narrative review with no new data. It argues that the way people use words, especially function words such as pronouns, articles and negations, works as a stable individual-difference marker. Their reliability evidence is moderate. Successive 2-minute speech segments correlate at r = 0.51 across 21 categories. Four-week test-retest correlations of everyday speech are 0.41 for standard linguistic categories and only 0.24 for psychological-process categories. The link to personality is weak. Big Five self-reports correlate with word use at r = 0.10 to 0.16 in a few hundred students. Neuroticism goes with more negative-emotion words, fewer positive-emotion words and more first-person singular. Depression is tied to "I" specifically, not me, my or mine. Emotion words make up under 5% of all words, so emotion counts are a weak readout of emotional state. Raters who judge a text's emotionality agree with its language more closely than the writers' own self-reports do. The authors also note that word counts ignore context and irony.

For Paul's systems, this is the stated source for the Pennebaker LIWC base in the affective-N slot, and through Pennebaker and King (1999) for the fallback trait weights in the lexical Big Five. As built, both of those direct uses are now dormant or have moved. Since round 7b, the LIWC base in affective N is only a convergent-validity anchor (r = +.24) and is no longer part of the score. The Pennebaker–King weights in big5_traits.py are overridden whenever mairesse_smoreg.json is present, and it is present. The review's main value here is calibration. With word-trait correlations of r = 0.10 to 0.16, a mean held-out r of .350 against RKH is more than this literature supports, which is consistent with the method-shared inflation the system already records. The low reliability of psychological-process categories also makes the system's failed cross-genre transfers unsurprising. The evidence comes from US college students writing spontaneously. It does not cover staff-written press or floor ritual.

bearings.paper_claim: Neuroticism relates to more negative-emotion words, fewer positive-emotion words and more first-person singular, with Big Five-word correlations of only r = 0.10 to 0.16 (Pennebaker & King 1999). Depression is tied to elevated 'I' specifically, not me/my/mine (Rude et al.). Emotion words are under 5% of words and weakly predict emotional state.
bearings.paper_location: The Big Five, p. 559; Depression and Suicidality, pp. 560-561; Which Words Should We Be Studying?, pp. 570-571
bearings.system_side: The LIWC base is z(first-person singular) + z(negemo) - z(posemo) over interview speech for members with at least 800 words. FPS counts i|me|my|mine|myself together, which is the pooling the paper says dilutes the depression signal. Since round 7b, the emitted affective_n is the E-residualized, party-controlled LLM facet score only; LIWC is kept as a convergent anchor (r = +.24, gate G3) and is not a component. The brain note (single-look-holdout-discipline-cases-2-3) still describes the measure as z(LIWC) + z(LLM).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence is college-student self-reports and spontaneous personal writing. Interview speech by media-trained legislators is a different genre and population, and no gold N criterion exists here. A LIWC-to-construct correlation near .24 is about what the paper's r = 0.10 to 0.16 range allows, so the anchor's modest size is expected and is not a defect. The I-only versus I+me+my distinction comes from a clinical depression sample and is untested for N in politicians.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests|Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests]]

bearings.paper_claim: Self-reported Big Five correlates with closed-vocabulary word use at only r = 0.10 to 0.16 (Pennebaker & King 1999, several hundred students, multiple writing samples). The directions are neuroticism to negemo and I, extraversion to posemo and social, and agreeableness to posemo and low negemo.
bearings.paper_location: Traditional Personality Measures, The Big Five, p. 559
bearings.system_side: The hand weights W cite 'Pennebaker-King / Yarkoni / Mairesse correlates' (for example, ES: anx -.30, negemo -.25, i -.20). They are a dormant fallback, because fec/liwc/mairesse_smoreg.json exists and replaces them, and Empath .dic lists replace the exemplar word lists. The reported held-out CV against RKH has a mean of .350 (E .510).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's ceiling applies to text matched against self-report in students. RKH targets are themselves derived from text, so .35 against RKH is not comparable evidence of validity. The gap between .35 and the paper's 0.10-0.16 is consistent with the method-shared inflation the component already lists as an assumption. Hand-weight signs carry over only if the fallback is ever reactivated.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)|Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Word use was internally consistent across text types for 36 LIWC dimensions and stable across settings, but four-week retest reliability was 0.41 for standard linguistic variables and only 0.24 for psychological-process variables (EAR, 52 students). Successive 2-minute speech intervals correlated at 0.51.
bearings.paper_location: Psychometric Properties of Word Use, pp. 555-556
bearings.system_side: The genre-residualized refit requires same-trait cross-genre r to exceed cross-trait within-genre |r| (an MTMM bar), which the parent family failed. Interview affective N failed to transfer to floor and hearing text (rho .050, .161). RITUAL stripping removes chamber boilerplate before counting.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's cross-context consistency comes from personal diaries, essays and everyday talk, all self-authored. Congressional floor, press and social text is partly staff-written and ritualized, which is outside the paper's scope. The low reliability of psychological-process categories (0.24) predicts weak genre transfer for the emotion and cognition categories that carry N and A. The system's own results are therefore the binding evidence, and the paper does not overturn them.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)|Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Emotion words make up under 5% of words in speech and writing, so emotion-word counts are weak predictors of emotional state. Word counts cannot capture context, irony or sarcasm. Judges' ratings of text emotionality track language more closely than authors' self-reports.
bearings.paper_location: Which Words Should We Be Studying?, pp. 570-571; Summary, pp. 554-555, 572
bearings.system_side: Per-release intensity is |lsd_net|/words (or charge = (pos+neg)/words), multiplied by the stance sign to give press_value. That makes intensity a scale factor on every press cell.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's claim concerns personal emotional state, not how heated a policy release is, and LSD2015 is a political-news dictionary rather than LIWC. Its sparsity point does carry over: in short releases a few dictionary hits set the multiplier. The judge-rating finding supports the component's open question of validating intensity against human-coded intensity rather than assuming it.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity|Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity]]

bearings.paper_claim: In two studies, judges' ratings of emotionality correlated more strongly with the language of the texts than the writers' or speakers' self-reports did, which raises the question of which personality 'gold standard' to use.
bearings.system_side: Validity is judged against observer panels (Senate academics and insiders) and RKH. The system records an A-ES correlation of about .44, of which about .21 is attributed to text-tone halo, and runs halo-removal and A-ES bars.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Observer panels rate senators partly from the same public speech the text readers score. Convergence with judges can therefore reflect shared observable cues rather than the trait itself, which is the halo mechanism the system already tests. No coefficients are given, the evidence is only two studies, and the domain is emotion rather than Big Five panels.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Big Five validation against Senate gold panels and criteria|Big Five validation against Senate gold panels and criteria]]

gaps_exposed: Function-word style is a gap. The paper treats pronoun and particle shifts (I to we, exclusive words, articles) as the most informative signal, but the stance and press layers use only content dictionaries (LSD) and NLI. No style-based signal exists, and none has been validated. This is listed as a gap only and is not a recommendation.

Transient event windows are not handled. Shared upheavals raised first-person plural by 135% and cut 'I' by 12% for about a week, returning to baseline by day 10. The trait readers pool text across time with no exclusion window around shocks, so crisis-period speech could move member-level N or E scores.

There is no linguistic-synchrony measure. The paper shows turn-by-turn function-word matching in dyads (Niederhoffer & Pennebaker 2002). The co-appearance layer records only that two members appeared together, not whether their speech converged. Any such measure would be UNVERIFIED new analysis until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

Ghost-writing and genre authorship are not modelled. The paper's individual-difference claims rest on self-authored spontaneous text, and the system has no per-genre authorship weight beyond C_INT_W and RITUAL stripping.
flags: Brain note concepts/single-look-holdout-discipline-cases-2-3-n-slot-and-gold-template.md describes affective_n as z(Pennebaker LIWC base) + z(LLM facets), and it gives the emitter path as fec/emit_affective_n.py. The live code at fec/members/emit_affective_n.py:39-43,56 emits the E-residualized, party-controlled LLM score only, with LIWC as an anchor. The note is stale on both points and the component description repeats the error.

The component assumption 'Negative-emotion and first-person-singular words track N (Pennebaker)' overstates the source. The paper reports r = 0.10 to 0.16 against student self-reports, and its depression evidence is specific to 'I', while the system's FPS regex pools me/my/mine/myself.

big5_traits.py:177-178 labels W as 'Pennebaker–King / Yarkoni / Mairesse correlates', but those weights are dormant because mairesse_smoreg.json overrides them. Citations of Pennebaker for the live lexical weights would be inaccurate.
paul_alignment: Paul left no annotations on this paper. His positions on affective-n ('No annotation addresses it directly', citing Ramey) and lexical-big5 (Ramey 'dated but foundational'; Birkenmaier's criticism of unvalidated SVM) are consistent with what this review shows. The review supplies the modest effect-size ceiling (r = 0.10 to 0.16) that Paul's notes lack, and it supports his preference for venue-specific frameworks, since its reliability evidence comes from self-authored student text. Paul is not stale here, but the brain's description of the affective-N measure is stale (see flags).

related.why: This is a meta-analysis of Big Five–LIWC correlations that updates the r = 0.10 to 0.16 figures this review reports from Pennebaker & King (1999).
Ramey applies LIWC-style closed-vocabulary trait measurement to congressional speech, carrying this review's method to politicians. It is the template for the system's lexical Big Five.
It addresses this review's limitation that general dictionaries ignore domain context by building corpus-specific sentiment dictionaries.
It pairs a dictionary with crowd-coded judgments, in line with this review's finding that judge ratings track language more closely than self-reports.
It validates computational trait measures (agency and communion) for politicians, the elite-population validation that this student-based review lacks.
It measures the emotional intensity of congressional speech through vocal pitch rather than emotion-word counts, which this review shows are sparse at under 5% of words.

backlinks.why: Marrero's theoretical basis for links between language and personality. It is also the source of the system's first-person and negative-emotion anchor for affective-N.
The Pennebaker LIWC and Essays lineage (Pennebaker & King 1999) is the survey's founding benchmark and the basis of the system's affective-N and lexical features.
LIWC word-category foundations (negemo, first-person singular) behind both Celli's cues and the system's affective-N anchor.

extraction.research_question: Estimate the mean predictive validity (Pearson r) of social-media digital footprints for each Big 5 trait; test whether the types of footprint used, the platform's default privacy setting (public vs. private), and study quality moderate prediction accuracy; check for publication bias; and assess whether accuracy is consistent across traits (Abstract; Sec. 1.3, p.151).
extraction.theory: Social-media content is an extension of "one's self" and reflects actual personality rather than idealized self-presentation (Back et al., 2010; Seidman, 2013), so digital footprints should carry personality signal (Sec. 1.1, p.150). Benchmark: the typical behavior-personality correlation of about 0.30-0.40, the "personality coefficient" (Meyer et al., 2001; Roberts et al., 2007), which the authors call the "correlational upper-limit" (Abstract; Sec. 4, p.155). The Big 5 (McCrae & Costa, 1987; McCrae & John, 1992) is the target framework (Sec. 1.2, p.151). No formal theory of why particular footprints predict particular traits is developed; the moderator hypotheses come from survey literature on demographics and from the extraversion-activity link.
extraction.data: Unit: independent study-level effect size. Literature (Scopus, ISI Web of Science, PubMed, ProQuest, plus Google/Google Scholar and citation chasing), search finalized May 2017 (Sec. 2.1, p.151-152). 24 papers and 28 studies identified (Sec. 3.1, p.154). Removed 12 studies for non-independence: 11 used MyPersonality (Facebook) data, plus Golbeck (2016) Study 3 (shared data with Golbeck et al., 2011). Final set: 14 papers, 16 independent studies, 80 effect sizes (16 per trait). Platforms in the 16: Facebook 7, Twitter 5, Sina Weibo 3, Instagram+Twitter 1. Footprints: 9 single-type studies, 7 multiple-type. Five papers lacked usable effect sizes; author contact recovered one; four were excluded (Sec. 2.4, p.153). Participant N and study years are not reported in the extracted text; the pooled N is not stated. Coders: the authors, with full agreement reported (Sec. 2.4, p.154).
extraction.method:
Five separate random-effects meta-analyses, one per Big 5 trait, using untransformed Pearson r (Fisher z explicitly rejected, citing Schmidt & Hunter, 2014; Sec. 2.4, p.153). Conversions: R^2 to r by square root (n=2); AUROC to Cohen's d to r (n=1); sensitivity/specificity or PPV/NPV to odds ratio to d to r (n=1); non-r reports converted (n=4). Where a study had several models or features, the best model or highest feature effect was used (Sec. 2.4, p.152-153). Outliers: Grubbs test (none found). Heterogeneity: Q, tau^2, I^2. Publication bias: funnel plot, Begg-Mazumdar and Egger tests, trim-and-fill, classic fail-safe N. Moderators: univariate random-effects meta-regression, REML, alpha 0.05, p<0.10 discussed; a moderator was tested only if at least 4 studies per group (Fu et al., 2014). Quality groups were pooled as low+medium (2+2) vs high (12) to reach the minimum. Software: Comprehensive Meta-analysis v3.3.070 (Sec. 2.4, p.153-154; Sec. 3.2.3, p.154).</method>
<parameter name="identification">None causal. Observational meta-analysis. Moderators are coded study characteristics entered one at a time (univariate), so no moderator is adjusted for another. Coefficients reflect between-study associations, not within-study or individual-level effects.
extraction.scope: Population: social-media users in the 16 included studies, mostly English-speaking users or Sina Weibo (Chinese) users; the authors state that cultural comparison was not possible (Sec. 5, p.157). Platforms: Facebook, Twitter, Sina Weibo, Instagram (combined with Twitter). Era: literature up to May 2017. Institutions: not applicable (no institutional sampling). Measures are from 2012-2017-era studies.

key_findings.finding: Mean meta-analytic correlations between digital footprints and each Big 5 trait (random effects, 16 effect sizes per trait). Extraversion highest, agreeableness lowest; the authors report no significant differences across traits, though no formal cross-trait test is named.
key_findings.location: Sec. 3.2.1, p.154; Abstract p.150; Table 2 p.157; cross-trait claim Sec. 4, p.155

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity is large and mostly true between-study variance. Q is significant for every trait, but tau^2 is small.
No evidence of publication bias. Funnel plots symmetric; trim-and-fill added no studies; fail-safe N exceeds the 5k+10 rule of thumb for all traits.
Grubbs outlier test flagged no studies.
key_findings.numbers: 0 studies removed.

key_findings.finding: Multiple types of footprints are associated with higher accuracy for O, C and N (significant). E shows a non-significant trend. A shows no increase (the text says 'except agreeableness' but gives no coefficient). The Abstract's 'accuracy improves' claim rests on these trait-level results.
Demographics (age, gender) are associated with higher accuracy for agreeableness and neuroticism, and a marginal increase for openness.
Activity statistics (friends, posts, network density) are associated with higher accuracy for extraversion only at a marginal level.

Language/text features and pictures did not improve accuracy over other footprint types. Public vs. private default platform setting had no significant effect. Study quality had no significant effect.
key_findings.numbers: Platform: private (Facebook) vs public (Twitter, Weibo, Reddit, Instagram): no significant effect. Quality: high n=12 vs low+medium n=4 (2+2): no significant effect.

key_findings.finding: Likes were not testable as a moderator, since only one study used them. The one Likes study in the pool is coded but not moderator-tested.
key_findings.numbers: Likes moderator: 1 study.

key_findings.finding: Non-independence screening removed about 43% of identified studies, mostly MyPersonality Facebook studies. Facebook dominates the remaining evidence base only partly: 7 of 16 included studies.
key_findings.numbers: 12 of 28 studies excluded (11 MyPersonality + 1 Golbeck 2016 Study 3). Included: Facebook 7, Twitter 5, Sina Weibo 3, Instagram+Twitter 1.

limitations: Few studies per platform: no thorough cross-platform comparison of accuracy (Sec. 5, p.157).
Heterogeneity in features and analytic approaches prevented estimating the contribution of individual features to accuracy (Sec. 5, p.157).
Cultural differences could not be tested; samples are mostly English-speaking or Sina Weibo (Chinese) users (Sec. 5, p.157).
Visual footprints: only a minority of studies used pictures, none used video, and only one (Skowron et al., 2016) used Instagram or Snapchat, so visual results are preliminary (Sec. 5, p.157).
Privacy: only default platform settings were coded; the users' actual privacy settings were not collected, so the null platform result should be treated with caution (Sec. 4, p.155).

Study quality is an approximation from source rank (Scopus CiteScore quartile; CORE 2017 and Microsoft Academic conference ranks), because no standard quality guidelines exist for this field (Sec. 2.3.3, p.152).
Moderator tests are underpowered: groups need at least 4 studies, and effects with p<0.10 are discussed (Sec. 2.4, p.154; Sec. 3.2.3, p.154).
Five papers lacked usable effect sizes; one author supplied data and four were excluded. The text does not say whether those four were among the 16 included studies (Sec. 2.4, p.153).
Only 16 independent studies were included, and 11 of the 12 non-independent studies were excluded for overlap with MyPersonality data (Sec. 3.1, p.154).
Coverage and era: search finalized May 2017; default privacy settings are expected to change over time (Sec. 4, p.155).

short_quotes.quote: Overall, the present meta-analysis demonstrates that Big 5 personality traits can be inferred using digital footprints extracted from social media with remarkable accuracy.
digital records of behaviors on social media may represent a quite reliable source of information for the prediction
accuracy improves when analyses include demographics and multiple types of digital footprints.

measures: Self-report Big 5 criteria: Big Five Inventory (John & Srivastava, 1999; John, Naumann & Soto, 2008), 10-item BFI (Gosling, Rentfrow & Swann, 2003), TIPI (Table 1), and IPIP (Goldberg et al., 2006).
Effect size: Pearson r, converted from R^2, AUROC (via Cohen's d), sensitivity/specificity or PPV/NPV (via odds ratio), and other reported statistics.

Digital-footprint codes (yes/no per study): demographics; Facebook Likes; user activity statistics (posts, friends, network density, received Likes, comments, tags); language/text features; pictures; multiple vs. single type.
Platform: public default (Twitter, Sina Weibo, Reddit, Instagram) vs. private default (Facebook).
Study quality: high/medium/low from Scopus CiteScore 2016 quartile (journals) or CORE 2017 / Microsoft Academic ranking (conference proceedings).
Heterogeneity and bias statistics: Q, tau^2, tau, I^2; Begg-Mazumdar; Egger; trim-and-fill; fail-safe N.

summary_md:
Azucar, Marengo and Settanni (Personality and Individual Differences 124, 2018; online December 2017) pooled 16 independent studies from 14 papers. They ran one random-effects meta-analysis per trait on untransformed Pearson r. The criterion in every study was a self-report Big Five inventory (BFI, TIPI or IPIP) from ordinary users of Facebook, Twitter, Sina Weibo or Instagram, with literature searched up to May 2017. The pooled correlations were: Openness .39, Conscientiousness .35, Extraversion .40, Agreeableness .29 (the lowest) and Neuroticism .33. The authors found no publication bias. Heterogeneity was very large (I² ≥ 93.15, every Q(15) significant). In univariate meta-regressions, using several types of footprint raised accuracy for O, C and N. Adding demographics raised it for A and N. Activity statistics (friends, posts, network density) raised it for E only marginally (β .19, p .06). Text and pictures alone added nothing. The pooled numbers are optimistic, because each study contributed its best model or strongest feature.

For Paul's systems this is a calibration paper, not a validation of them. Melange scores members of Congress, whose posts and press output are written by staff, against RKH estimates, which are themselves derived from text, and against Senate expert and insider panels. Neither of those is self-report from the members. The lexical reader's held-out CV against RKH has a mean of .350. That sits inside Azucar's range by coincidence of scale, not by comparable design, so it should never be presented as matching the meta-analytic benchmark. The paper offers three sharper lessons:
- Agreeableness is the least recoverable trait from digital footprints, which supports the system's move from lexical A to behavioural cooperation.
- Activity counts are at best a marginal Extraversion signal.
- Demographics improve "accuracy" only because group membership correlates with self-reported traits. The system's affective-N gate removes exactly that signal on purpose.

These pooled figures cover 16 studies of lay users and are UNSTRATIFIED across platforms. The authors could not test differences between platforms.

bearings.paper_claim: Digital footprints predict self-reported Big Five at pooled r = O .39, C .35, E .40, A .29, N .33 (16 studies per trait, random effects). Heterogeneity is extreme (I² 93.15-97.46). Each study contributed its best model or highest single-feature effect. The 'extension of self' premise (Back et al. 2010) is the theoretical warrant.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.150; Sec. 2.4 p.152-153 (best-model selection); Sec. 3.2.1 p.154; Table 2 p.157; Sec. 1.1 p.150
bearings.system_side: The reader builds a Ramey-style closed-vocabulary linear model over each member's tweet/post corpus plus floor and interview speech. It cites Birkenmaier for treating social posts as cue carriers and z-scores relative to this corpus only. Held-out CV against RKH: E .510, A .406, C .363, ES .258, O .214 (mean .350). O was reversed on the party check.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The pooled r values do not carry over as a benchmark. (1) Azucar's criterion is self-report from lay users, while the system's is RKH, which is text-derived and shares Mairesse-LIWC with the reader, so agreement is inflated. (2) Congressional accounts are staff-managed, which breaks the 'extension of self' premise. (3) Best-model selection and I² ≥ 93% mean a pooled .35 is not an expected accuracy for any one new setting. Any comparison must carry the label UNSTRATIFIED (16 studies, 4 platforms, 2012-2017 lay users). The trait ordering is also inverted: O is the best-predicted trait in Azucar but the weakest and party-reversed one here. That suggests the congressional O signal reflects genre or party rather than the person.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)|Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Agreeableness is the least recoverable trait from footprints (r = .29 [.21, .36]). It gained no accuracy from using several footprint types and improved only when demographics were added (β = .25, R² = .19).
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3.2.1 p.154; Sec. 3.2.3 p.154-155; Discussion Sec. 4 p.155
bearings.system_side: The lexical basis gives A the largest susceptibility weight (susc = .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E). The default behavioural basis replaces the A slot with cooperation_v2 after the nomological prereg indicted the lexical Big Five. RECEPT_TRAITS=lexical reverts.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This indirectly supports keeping the behavioural default and not reverting to lexical A. A is the weakest footprint trait even among lay users, where self-presentation is authentic. Transfer to legislators is weaker still: the paper concerns predictive validity against self-report, not whether A predicts yielding to pressure, which remains unvalidated here (no prospective H2 look).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Receptivity layer (susceptibility, incentive, prospect domain, seed probability)|Receptivity layer (susceptibility, incentive, prospect domain, seed probability)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Including demographics (age, gender) is associated with higher prediction accuracy for N (β = .25, p < .05, R² = .19) and A (β = .25, R² = .19).
bearings.system_side: affective_n is the LLM affective facets residualized on E and then on party, then z-scored. Its gate requires party r ≈ .000. The aim is construct integrity, not predictive accuracy.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Azucar's gain comes from group membership correlating with self-reported traits, a predictive shortcut. Adding party or gender as predictors would raise apparent accuracy while reintroducing the group signal the gate removes on purpose. Do not adopt it. The paper also uses univariate moderators between studies, with no adjustment, so the finding says nothing about individual-level confounding.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests|Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests]]

bearings.paper_claim: Studies using user-activity statistics (posts, friends, network density) show higher accuracy for Extraversion only at a marginal level (β = .19, R² = .18, p = .06). No other trait improved.
bearings.system_side: visibility_z (log counts of interviews and interview programs, from members with at least 3 attributed interviews) is used as the E-sociability role. Dominance comes from turn statistics plus leadership.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Activity volume links to E only, and only marginally (between studies, p = .06, small k). For legislators, interview counts are scheduled by press offices and track seniority and leadership, so this is weak support at most. It agrees with the brain's indictment of lexical E as 'broadcast talkativeness', which reads volume as a trait rather than a measured construct.

bearings.paper_claim: Studies combining several footprint types show higher accuracy for O (β = .27, R² = .16), C (β = .25, R² = .20) and N (β = .21, R² = .14). E shows a non-significant trend (p = .08) and A shows no gain. Text or pictures alone add nothing.
bearings.system_side: The v3 hybrid ridge-combines lexical featz, 8 interaction-channel features and agency/communion persona cues per trait. Its target is behavioural, it uses nested 5-fold CV, and it reports an honest held-out r.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This gives directional support for combining footprint types over relying on lexical rates alone, and it suggests the gain should appear in O, C and N rather than A. The evidence is a between-study meta-regression on self-report criteria. The hybrid targets behavioural criteria in a small elite sample, so any gain still needs a single pre-registered look. Per DE-062 it stays UNVERIFIED until reproduced by a second path.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#LLM item-level reader (Pink), ridge hybrid and CT-CM latent model|LLM item-level reader (Pink), ridge hybrid and CT-CM latent model]]

gaps_exposed: No self-report criterion exists for legislators. The system's references (RKH text estimates, Senate expert and insider panels) are not the criterion the footprint literature validates against, so the paper's accuracy figures cannot be imported as a benchmark.

Authorship: the system does not model staff or ghost-writing in social posts and press output, although the meta-analysis's theoretical warrant (content as an extension of the self) assumes the person wrote it.

Per-platform and per-genre accuracy: the paper could not stratify by platform, and the system pools tweets, floor speech and interviews into one corpus (BIG5_SOURCES restricts genres for validation only). No stratified accuracy by genre is reported against an external criterion.

Upward bias from model selection: the paper's best-model-per-study rule inflates pooled r. The system's own improvement rounds guard against this with single looks, but no comparison to a lay-user benchmark accounts for it.
flags: Do not quote 'remarkable accuracy' or pooled r ≈ .35 as evidence that Melange's lexical Big Five (CV vs RKH mean .350) is valid. The criteria differ, RKH shares the reader's method, and the pooled figure spans I² ≥ 93% heterogeneity. Any citation must carry the label UNSTRATIFIED (16 studies, 4 platforms, lay users, 2012-2017).

The demographics-moderator finding must not be used to justify adding party or gender as trait predictors. That conflicts with the affective-N gate (party-controlled, party r = .000) and would make a group proxy look like a personality measure.

The big5_traits.py docstring treats social posts as validated personality-cue carriers (citing Birkenmaier). Azucar's evidence concerns self-authored lay-user content, so it does not extend that claim to staff-managed congressional accounts.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals, D-021 or D-025: the paper makes no network-edge or influence claims.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. It agrees with his call for frameworks specific to each venue: the paper's platform heterogeneity is large and it could not test differences across platforms. It also fits his view that A collapses into a smaller set of observable dispositions. It does not support his more optimistic plan to use psychological traits as edge parameters in the receptivity layer. Even among lay users with authentic self-report, A is the least recoverable trait (r = .29), and the paper says nothing about whether traits predict yielding to pressure. His notes about the receptivity layer and lexical Big Five predate the nomological indictment and the behavioural basis now running in receptivity_layer.py. The paper agrees with the system as currently built more than with those older notes.

related.why: A later meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five relations, restricted to text. It gives per-category effect sizes for the closed-vocabulary features big5_traits.py actually uses, where Azucar pools across footprint types.
Ramey et al. apply closed-vocabulary trait scoring to legislators' speech without a self-report criterion, which is the elite setting Azucar's lay-user evidence does not cover.

Birkenmaier and Lechner validate measures of politicians' public personality (agency and communion) from text. That is the system's cited warrant for social posts, and it rests on a different construct from Azucar's self-report criterion.
Big Five regression on Twitter footprints, the single-platform study design that Azucar pools.
Hargittai documents sampling biases in social-network-site data, which bear on Azucar's limitation that its samples were mostly English-speaking or Weibo users.
A review of threats and challenges in personality computing, including validity and ethics, that overlaps Azucar's discussion.
A more recent survey of ML and deep-learning trait detection that covers the post-2017 methods outside Azucar's search window.

backlinks.why: Meta-analysis of predicting the Big Five from social media footprints. It benchmarks how weak Celli's 0.625 accuracy and 0.578 F1 are.

meta.title: Do Redistricting Commissions Avoid Partisan Gerrymanders?
meta.venue: American Politics Research 50(3):379-395 (copyright 2021; online first). Metadata hint confirmed. Author affiliations: Binghamton University (Best, Magleby, McDonald); Kutztown University of Pennsylvania (Lem).

extraction.title: Do Redistricting Commissions Avoid Partisan Gerrymanders?
extraction.venue: American Politics Research 50(3):379-395 (copyright 2021; online first). Metadata hint confirmed. Author affiliations: Binghamton University (Best, Magleby, McDonald); Kutztown University of Pennsylvania (Lem).
extraction.coverage: Read the full text in full: the entire extracted file _text/7d1eedcb2296.txt (2,283 lines, about 80,140 chars), covering front matter, abstract, introduction, commission forms and rules (Tables 1-3), gerrymander identification framework, data, evaluations (Figures 2-3), state case studies (AZ, NJ, VA; Table 4; Figure 4), conclusion, appendix (neutral map algorithm, VRA handling, compactness, Table A for CA/IA/NY/WA), notes 1-18 and references. Paul's markup: no markup or annotation files were supplied for this item ("(none)"), so paul_markup is empty. Path-finding, lobbying, network and text-measurement content: none present in this paper.
extraction.research_question: Do redistricting commissions used in the 2010 round produce congressional district maps that are biased toward one party compared with a neutral, partisan-blind standard drawn within the same state? The paper asks how well commissions perform as neutral decision makers, using the 2010 round as the test.
extraction.theory: Gerrymandering harms two things: (1) exclusion or silencing of minority-party voters via vote cracking (exclusionary gerrymander, indicated by a smaller-than-expected standard deviation in district vote shares with minimal minority opportunity to win), and (2) entrenchment of a majority party regardless of its vote share via packing (indicated by skew in the district vote distribution, median minus mean). Total electoral bias = turnout bias + gerrymandering bias (asymmetry due to skew). Commissions are expected to act like a divided government, with bipartisan members producing bias toward whichever side gains an upper hand, or to produce neutral lines if bipartisanship works (pp. 381-383, 384, 390).
extraction.data: Unit: state congressional district plans (enacted maps) and statewide two-party vote returns by voter tabulation district (VTD). Sample: 34 states that could be evaluated, of which 7 use commissions (independent: AZ, CA, WA; advisory: IA, NY, VA; politician: NJ). Excluded 16 states: 12 with one or two districts, KY and OR (no VTD data), OK and WV (insufficient partisan predictability). Period: 2010 redistricting round; elections analyzed 2008-2014 in Table 4 and Table A (e.g., AZ 2008-2012 statewide, NJ 2008-2013, VA 2008-2013); the text also cites 2016-2020 House results for AZ and VA. Simulated baseline: 10,000 computer-generated plans per state. Vote data: Daily Kos (Wolf) estimates disaggregating county returns to VTDs using 2008 presidential shares; Census VTD shapefiles. Validation of vote estimates against official VTD tallies in WI, NC, FL: correlations 0.87-0.97 (p. 383). N for the sample: 34 states, 7 commission states, 10,000 maps per state (~340,000 simulated plans).
extraction.method: Descriptive counterfactual-comparison design with a simulated neutral baseline. Each enacted map is compared with the distribution of outcomes from 10,000 partisan-blind plans per state, generated with the Magleby and Mosesson (2018) multi-level weighted graph-partitioning algorithm (rook contiguity, population balance within about plus or minus 1%, compactness considered in the appendix). Indicators: observed vs expected standard deviation of Democratic district vote share (exclusion); observed vs expected gerrymandering bias (median minus mean district vote share, skew/entrenchment); turnout bias (mean district vote share minus statewide vote share); observed vs expected number of districts won by the statewide Democratic candidate (majority-rule test). Evaluation is on average values across states and elections (Figures 2-3), then state-by-state (Table 4, Figure 4 traces of observed vs expected district vote shares, sorted low to high). For Arizona, the two Hispanic majority-minority districts were held fixed in all simulated plans (Appendix, VRA section). Compactness compared via dispersion (area / minimum circumscribing circle) and perimeter (Niemi et al. 1990) ratios for 1,000 simulated maps vs the commission map.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The comparison to a neutral within-state simulated baseline is the counterfactual for how a partisan-blind process would sort voters across districts given residential geography. Cross-state comparisons are explicitly rejected because geography differs across states (p. 380). The paper does not estimate treatment effects of commissions versus legislatures using a causal design; its cross-state commission-vs-legislature comparison (Figures 2-3) is descriptive.
extraction.scope: Population: 34 states with at least three congressional districts and usable VTD data, US House districts, 2010 redistricting round. Institutions: 7 states with redistricting commissions (3 independent, 3 advisory, 1 politician commission; the paper labels NJ politician and Hawaii politician; see Table 1), plus legislative and court-imposed plans in other states. Era: post-2010 maps used in 2012-2014 House elections (with later 2016-2020 references for AZ and VA). Scope is congressional, not state legislative, districts.

key_findings.finding: Three of seven commission states produced suspect results benefiting one party: Arizona pro-Democratic; New Jersey and Virginia pro-Republican. Commissions generally produce less partisan bias than legislatures, but do not always eliminate it.
key_findings.location: Abstract p. 379; Introduction pp. 380-381; Evaluations p. 385-386
key_findings.numbers: 3 of 7 commission states flagged; 34 states evaluated; 10,000 simulated maps per state

key_findings.finding: Across the 34 evaluated states, maps enacted by commission states generally perform better (closer to neutral baseline) than maps enacted by states without commissions.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative; commission states mostly near or below the 45-degree lines; AZ, NJ, VA above the line in Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Arizona (independent commission): turnout bias favored Democrats about 2 points across all 10 statewide 2008-2012 elections. Enacted plan added roughly 1.5 points of pro-Democratic asymmetry bias beyond what residential patterns would produce, erasing a neutral pro-Republican asymmetry. Republicans charged mistreatment and the commission's map was judged a pro-Democratic gerrymander.
key_findings.location: Suspect 1, pp. 387-388; Table 4 p. 387; Conclusion p. 390
key_findings.numbers: turnout bias about +2 points; added asymmetry about +1.5 points; expected asymmetry balanced by pro-Republican bias under neutral drawing

key_findings.finding: Arizona: enacted standard deviations were consistently larger than expected (more dispersed, less competitive districts), with packing in both directions; Democrats carried the three CDs they were described as making more competitive. The contramajoritarian result was limited: Republicans won 5 of 9 seats in 2014 and 2016, so Democrats were not entrenched.
key_findings.numbers: Obama 2012 at 45.4% of two-party vote carried 5 of 9 seats; Democratic Senate candidate 48.4% in 2012 would have carried 5 of 9 seats with CDs 1, 2, 9 over 50%; Republicans won 5 of 9 House seats in 2014 and 2016

key_findings.finding: New Jersey (political commission, party-line 7-6 vote favored the Republican plan): enacted lines show an anti-Democratic gerrymander bias of 1.7 to 3.7 points, partly offset by 1.3 to 2.5 points of pro-Democratic turnout bias. Standard deviations uniformly larger than the neutral average.
key_findings.location: Suspect 2, p. 389; Table 4 p. 387; Conclusion p. 391
key_findings.numbers: gerrymander bias against Democrats 1.7-3.7 points; turnout bias +1.3 to +2.5; 2013 Senate special: Democrat 55.5% carried 6 of 12 districts

key_findings.finding: Virginia (advisory commission, plan actually chosen by the legislature after an inconclusive session and a 20-20 Senate tie broken by the Republican Lieutenant Governor): a pro-Republican gerrymander, persistently biased against Democrats in all 10 observed elections; asymmetry of 2.7-4.0 points; fewer than 1% of partisan-blind plans exceed the observed asymmetry, except Warner's abnormally lopsided 2008 Senate win.
key_findings.location: Suspect 3, pp. 389-390; Table 4 p. 387; Conclusion p. 390
key_findings.numbers: asymmetry bias 2.7-4.0 points against Democrats in 10 of 10 elections; Obama 2012 won 52% of two-party vote and carried 4 of 11 districts; Democrats won 3 of 11 House races in 2012 and 2014; 4 of 5 elections with Democratic vote share 50-54% failed to carry a majority of districts

key_findings.finding: California (independent) slightly reduced but did not eliminate anti-Democratic bias from residential patterns; Washington (independent) drew a plan that allowed residential-pattern consequences to stand; no evidence of gerrymandering in either. Iowa and New York maps fall in line with the neutral standard; Iowa may be somewhat more competitive than residential patterns alone.
key_findings.location: Suspect discussion pp. 386-387 and Conclusion pp. 390; Table A p. 392
key_findings.numbers: CA 53 districts; IA 4 districts (55% vote share won all four seats by both parties per text); NY 27 districts (2010 Comptroller: Democrat 52% carried 11 of 27)

key_findings.finding: Commissions do well on charges (population equality, contiguity, compactness, jurisdictional boundaries, competitiveness) and produce maps closer to the partisan-blind standard than legislatures, but the same cannot be said uniformly for avoiding partisan gerrymanders. The authors argue commissions are decidedly bipartisan, and that the charges given to them focus on form rather than a substantive anti-gerrymander standard.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative

key_findings.finding: Arizona's enacted map is compact on the dispersion measure relative to algorithm-drawn maps: its median district's dispersion ratio (0.4797) exceeds the median district in 95.8% of 1,000 simulated maps; simulated maps show lower variance in compactness than the commission map (86.95% lower on dispersion SD; 99.8% lower on perimeter SD).

limitations: Vote-share data are estimates: Daily Kos disaggregation of county returns to VTDs using 2008 presidential shares. Validation correlations of 0.87-0.97 were checked only against official VTD tallies in WI, NC, and FL (p. 383).
VTD shapefiles are out of date by the 2012 and 2014 elections because states re-precinct more often than they redistrict; the authors rely on estimated VTD vote totals (fn 10, p. 392).

Results are based on average values across states and elections in the first evaluation; the authors state a closer state-by-state look is required to say whether any suspect state enacted a partisan gerrymander (p. 386-387).
Only 2010-round congressional maps; 16 states excluded (12 with one or two districts, KY and OR lacking VTD data, OK and WV with low partisan predictability) (fn 12).

The neutral baseline imposes only minimalist constraints (contiguity, compactness, equal population, plus fixed Hispanic majority-minority districts in AZ). Simulated maps differ from enacted maps in other ways, and the compactness comparison shows algorithm maps are more uniform, not identical.
The sign/size of the residual bias is a within-state counterfactual; the paper does not claim causal effects of commission design.

Threshold for 'suspect' is an informal statistical standard (observed vs expected values across 10,000 maps; e.g., less than 1% of simulated plans exceeding observed asymmetry); the paper notes standard deviation alone is insufficient to identify partisan gerrymanders because entrenchment requires packing and cracking together (fn 13).
Maryland and Utah are flagged as possible exclusionary (cracking) outliers in fn 13 but are not analyzed in depth.
measures: Statewide two-party Democratic vote share
Mean district vote share (equal-district weighting)
Median district vote share
Turnout bias = mean district vote share minus statewide vote share
Gerrymandering bias (asymmetry/skew) = median district vote share minus mean district vote share
Total electoral bias = turnout bias + gerrymandering bias
Observed vs expected standard deviation of district Democratic vote share (exclusion indicator; expected from 10,000 simulated maps)
Observed vs expected number of districts won by statewide Democratic candidate (majority-rule test)
Compactness: dispersion (district area / minimum circumscribing circle area) and perimeter (district area / area of circle with same perimeter), per Niemi et al. 1990
Observed vs expected gerrymander bias from simulated plans
